request.system: You are an expert in clinical classification systems.

messages.content:
ICD-10-AM is the Australian modification of the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, 10th revision. Its disease codes are arranged in chapters, and a three-character category is written as one capital letter followed by two digits. The letter indicates the chapter or block: A and B are infectious diseases, C is malignant neoplasms, D is other neoplasms and blood disorders, E is endocrine, nutritional and metabolic disease, F is mental and behavioural disorders, G is the nervous system, H is the eye and ear, I is the circulatory system, J is the respiratory system, K is the digestive system, L is the skin, M is the musculoskeletal system, N is the genitourinary system, O is pregnancy and childbirth, P is the perinatal period, Q is congenital malformations, R is symptoms and abnormal findings, S and T are injury and poisoning, and Z is factors influencing health status. The two digits narrow the chapter to a specific category, for example J44 is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and N17 is acute kidney failure.

The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Using that structure, assign the three-character ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. Choose the chapter letter first, then the two digits.

Hospital course:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
Name: [redacted]
Age: 2 years
Sex: Female
Date of Admission: February 5, 2020
Date of Discharge: February 10, 2020
Admitting Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the hospital on February 5, 2020 for intermittent fever and dry cough. She had previously received oral medications for three days consisting of Tamiflu and Cefaclor. The patient's aunt was a suspected case of COVID-19 and had developed symptoms on January 26, 2020. She passed away on February 1, 2020. The physical examination on admission showed a temperature of 38.8°C, pulse of 110 beats per minute, respiration of 25 breaths per minute, and SpO2 of 100%. The results of the nasopharyngeal swab sample taken on admission were negative for SARS-CoV-2.

Diagnostic Results:
The chest computed tomography (CT) showed patchy and flocculent slightly high-density shadows in both lungs. The blood routine results revealed a leukocyte count of 9.29 × 109/L and lymphocytes of 1.63 × 109/L. C-reactive protein was 5 mg/L. The serum IgM antibody of influenza A was weakly positive. The third nasopharyngeal swab sample was also negative. However, the serum collected on February 5, 2020 was found to be positive for both IgG and IgM antibodies against SARS-CoV-2.
Final Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Treatment:
The patient was treated with Tamiflu continuously.

Disposition and Condition on Discharge:
The patient was discharged on February 10, 2020 with a return to normal body temperature. 

Follow-up Recommendations:
The patient was advised to undergo follow-up testing to ensure a complete recovery.

Answer in the form CODE: <letter><digit><digit>

text:
**CODE: J12**

This is a viral pneumonia. The admission features (fever, dry cough, and patchy bilateral lung shadows on CT) point to a lower respiratory tract infection, and the serology points to a viral cause (SARS-CoV-2 IgG and IgM positive, influenza A IgM weakly positive), with the nasopharyngeal swabs negative. The withheld final diagnosis prevents certainty.

In current ICD-10-AM, a confirmed COVID-19 episode would be coded to the U07 "special purposes" block, which is not among the chapters you listed. Within the listed chapters, J12 (viral pneumonia, unspecified) is the best fit.
